ai.literal: Without withholding, gladly who give, those who are like eyes, even from them, not begging ten million is worth.
ai.translation: Even from those who are as precious as one's own eyes and give gladly without withholding, not begging is worth ten million.
ai.modern: தன்னிடம் உள்ளதை மறைக்காமல் மகிழ்ந்து கொடுக்கும் கண் போன்றவர்களிடமும் பிச்சை கேட்காமல் இருப்பது ஒருவனுக்கு கோடி மடங்கு நன்மையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme dignity of self-reliance by stating that one should not beg even from the most generous and loving people. The phrase 'கண் அன்னார்' compares such willing givers to one's own precious eyes, highlighting their closeness and immense value. 'கரவாது உவந்து ஈயும்' describes their nature of giving joyfully without hiding their wealth. Yet, the poet asserts that 'இரவாமை' (not begging) even from them is worth ten million ('கோடி உறும்'), showing that preserving one's self-respect is far superior to receiving even the most willingly given charity.

ai.literal: Even by begging living a life if it is required, wandering let him perish, he who created the world.
ai.translation: If it is ordained that people must live even by begging, let the creator of the world wander and perish.
ai.modern: இரந்துதான் உயிர்வாழ வேண்டும் என்ற நிலை இருந்தால், இந்த உலகத்தைப் படைத்தவன் எங்கும் அலைந்து கெட்டொழியட்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet expresses a fierce condemnation of a world where begging is necessary for survival. The phrase 'irantum uyirvaazhtal veendin' sets the condition: if living requires one to beg. The poet then curses the creator of such a world ('ulaku iyatriyaan') with the words 'parantu keduka', meaning let him wander and perish just like a beggar. The strong language underscores the deep indignity of begging, suggesting that a world demanding such humiliation is fundamentally flawed and its maker deserves the same suffering.

ai.literal: Poverty's affliction having begged we will end saying than the hardness hard-natured thing there is not.
ai.translation: There is no hardness greater than the hard-hearted ignorance of saying, 'We will cure the affliction of poverty by begging.'
ai.modern: வறுமையின் துன்பத்தைப் பிச்சை எடுத்துத் தீர்ப்போம் என்று சொல்லும் வன்மையை விடக் கொடிய வன்மை வேறு இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet condemns the mindset of choosing to beg as a solution to poverty. The word inmai refers to poverty, and iṭumpai is the sorrow it brings. The poet states that resolving to cure this sorrow by begging shows a stubborn ignorance or hardness of heart. There is absolutely nothing harder or worse than this degrading resolution.

ai.literal: Space all not-containing nature-indeed space not-having time-even begging not-consenting greatness.
ai.translation: The nobility that refuses to beg even in times of utter destitution is of a magnitude that the entire world cannot contain.
ai.modern: வறுமையால் தன்னிடம் பொருள் இல்லாத காலத்திலும் பிறரிடம் சென்று இரந்து கேட்பதற்கு உடன்படாத பெருந்தன்மை, இந்த உலகம் முழுவதிலும் அடங்காத பெருமையை உடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet praises the immense dignity of those who refuse to beg. The word 'இடம்' is used twice with different meanings: first to mean the physical space of the whole world, and second to mean personal wealth or means. Even when one has absolutely nothing, the noble character that rejects begging is so vast and magnificent that the entire earth is too small to hold it.

ai.translation: Even if it is just thin gruel cooked with clear water, there is nothing sweeter than eating the food produced by one's own labor.

ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the dignity and joy of self-reliance. Thin gruel cooked with clear water represents the poorest of meals. Yet, if it is earned through one's own hard work, eating it brings a sweetness unmatched by any rich feast obtained through begging.

ai.literal: To the cow water saying even if begging, to the tongue than begging a disgraceful thing is not.
ai.translation: Even if one begs to provide water for a thirsty cow, there is nothing more disgraceful to the tongue than the act of begging.
ai.modern: ஒரு பசுவிற்கு நீர் வேண்டும் என்று பிறரிடம் இரந்து கேட்டாலும், ஒருவருடைய நாவிற்கு இரப்பதை விட இழிவான செயல் வேறு இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the absolute disgrace of begging, regardless of how noble the cause might be. The phrase 'ஆவிற்கு நீர்' (water for the cow) represents an extremely virtuous and urgent request, as providing water to a suffering animal is universally seen as a good deed. However, the word 'இரப்பினும்' (even if begging) shows that the act of asking itself taints the speaker. The tongue ('நாவிற்கு') is meant for dignified speech, and uttering words of supplication brings it unparalleled shame ('இளிவந்தது இல்'). Thus, begging is condemned unconditionally.

ai.literal: I will beg / those who beg / all / if begging / those who hide / do not beg / saying
ai.translation: I beg of all those who beg: if you must beg, do not beg from those who hide what they have.
ai.modern: பிச்சை எடுப்பவர்கள் எல்லாரிடமும் நான் ஒன்றை வேண்டிக் கேட்கிறேன்: நீங்கள் பிச்சை எடுத்தால், உள்ளதை மறைப்பவர்களிடம் சென்று பிச்சை எடுக்காதீர்கள்.
ai.explanation: The poet addresses beggars directly, making an earnest plea to them. The word 'இரப்பன்' (I beg) is used ironically to show the poet's sincerity in asking a favor of those who usually ask favors of others. He asks them that if they are forced by circumstances to beg ('இரப்பின்'), they should never beg from misers who hide their wealth ('கரப்பார்'). This highlights the extreme indignity of facing a miser's refusal, which is portrayed as worse than the act of begging itself.

ai.literal: Begging called safety without boat, concealment called rock to strike, split it will.
ai.translation: The unsafe boat called begging will split apart when it strikes the rock called refusal.
ai.modern: இரத்தல் என்னும் பாதுகாப்பற்ற படகு, இல்லை என்று மறைத்தல் என்னும் பாறை மோதினால் உடைந்து சிதறிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet uses a vivid metaphor to describe the precarious nature of begging. Begging is compared to a fragile boat that offers no real safety ('ஏமாப்பு இல் தோணி'). When a beggar asks for help and faces refusal, compared here to a hard rock of concealment ('கரவு என்னும் பார்'), the fragile boat shatters ('பக்கு விடும்'). This illustrates how the humiliation of being denied destroys the beggar's already fragile livelihood and self-worth.

ai.literal: Begging when thinking, heart will melt; concealment when thinking, even that which exists without will be destroyed.
ai.translation: The heart melts in sorrow at the mere thought of begging; but at the thought of someone concealing what they have to refuse a beggar, even one's very being is destroyed.
ai.modern: பிறரிடம் சென்று இரந்து கேட்பதை நினைத்தால் உள்ளம் உருகும்; ஆனால் தன்னிடம் இருப்பதை மறைத்து இல்லை என்று சொல்வதை நினைத்தால் உள்ள உயிரும் இல்லாமல் அழிந்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the deep sorrow of poverty with the greater moral failure of selfishness. The mere thought of having to beg makes a person's heart melt in shame and despair. However, the thought of someone deliberately concealing their wealth to refuse a beggar is so appalling that it destroys the very core of one's existence. The poet uses the melting of the heart to illustrate the pain of the seeker, and total destruction to condemn the cruelty of the one who withholds.

ai.literal: To those who withhold, where will hide, I wonder? Of those who beg, when speaking, departs life.
ai.translation: The life of those who beg departs the moment they utter their request. Where, I wonder, will the life of those who withhold their wealth hide?
ai.modern: இரப்பவர்கள் தம் தேவையைச் சொல்லும்போதே நாணத்தால் அவர்கள் உயிர் போய்விடுகிறது. அப்படியிருக்க, பொருளைத் தர மறுத்து மறைப்பவர்களின் உயிர் எங்கே சென்று ஒளிந்துகொள்ளுமோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the deep shame of the beggar with the callousness of the miser. When a person is forced to beg, the sheer humiliation of uttering the request causes their life or spirit to drain away. The poet then wonders where the life of the miser will hide when they selfishly withhold their wealth. If merely asking for help is enough to destroy a person's spirit, the act of denying that help must be an even greater burden on the soul.
